834.title: Jan Hus (1415)
834.hook: a Prague preacher burned at the Council of Constance, promised safe conduct
834.tomorrow: Thomas à Kempis in his cell
834.howItsDone: Jan Hus is remembered by Protestant churches as a forerunner of the Reformation and by the Moravian Church as part of its own story, and the Czech Republic marks a public day in his memory; the Catholic Church has expressed regret for his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wycliffe's Bible, copied by hand so ordinary people could hear scripture in English. Your line was the ploughman's bible. Which line did you carry out with you? Day eight hundred thirty-four.

A promise, on paper, with a seal. That's what the preacher carries when he leaves Prague. He has been summoned to a great church council in the city of Constance, to answer charges that his teaching is heresy. He has reason to be wary. But Sigismund, king and future emperor, has given him a letter of safe conduct: travel there, speak, and come home unharmed. So he goes. He believes he'll be allowed to explain himself. Before long, he's in prison. Today: Jan Hus.

Hus was a priest and teacher in Prague, and he preached in a chapel there in Czech, the language of the people in the pews, not only in Latin. He'd read Wycliffe, whose followers we met yesterday, and he shared some of his concerns: a church too tied to money and power, and scripture as the measure of it all. He preached hard against the sale of indulgences. Crowds came to hear him. And church authorities came to see him as dangerous. At Constance, the council demanded that he take back a list of teachings. Hus answered that some of them he had never taught, and that he couldn't swear to give up what he had never held, or to deny what he believed was true, unless someone showed him from scripture that he was wrong. The council judged him a heretic, and he was burned at the stake. Sigismund's safe conduct didn't save him. Christians remember Hus in different ways. Protestant histories have called him a forerunner of the Reformation, and the Moravian Church traces its roots to communities that grew from his followers. In the Czech lands he became a national figure. The Catholic Church, for its part, has in recent times expressed deep regret for his cruel death. Hus is remembered for words handed down under his name, which urge a Christian to seek the truth, love it, speak it, hold to it and defend it to death. They echo Jesus in the Gospel of John, in the King James Bible: "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
screen: `HE WOULD NOT DENY WHAT HE NEVER TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by a promise, even when others break theirs. Hus was let down by a promise. The practice turns that around. Think of one promise you've made that's become inconvenient. Helping someone move. Showing up for a friend. A commitment at work, or at home. Somebody else may have dropped theirs. Notice how much easier it would be to drop yours too. Then decide to keep it. The Psalms describe the person who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not." If you pray, you can ask for the strength to keep your word. If you don't, just hold the promise, and let it stay. The bell holds the time.
Jan Hus. A Prague preacher who would not deny what he believed true, and was burned at the Council of Constance despite a promise of safe conduct.
Your line: seek the truth. Today, keep the promise you thought of, and when you're tempted to shade the truth to make something easier, say the plain thing instead. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: Thomas à Kempis in his cell
835.hook: a quiet copyist-monk, and a small book on following Christ
835.carry: in a nook with a book
835.howItsDone: Christians of several traditions read The Imitation of Christ a short chapter at a time, often as part of a daily quiet time, and some copy out lines of scripture or devotional books by hand as a way of praying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jan Hus, holding to what he believed true after a promise to him was broken. Your line was seek the truth. Did you keep the promise you chose? Day eight hundred thirty-five.

Scratch, dip, scratch. A quill moving across parchment, a pot of ink, a window with gray light, and a man bent over a desk for hours, copying out the Bible, letter by letter. No printing press here. If a monastery wanted a book, someone like him made it by hand. The house is a small community of canons near the town of Zwolle, in what is now the Netherlands. The man rarely leaves. He prays with his brothers, copies books, guides the younger ones, and writes little pieces of his own. Nobody outside would call his life remarkable. Today: Thomas à Kempis in his cell.

Thomas belonged to a movement people called the Modern Devotion. Its idea was simple: a real, inner faith, lived out in ordinary days, by lay people and religious alike. Not great learning. Not grand projects. Prayer, humility, honest work, and walking after Christ. Out of that world came a small book, usually credited to Thomas, called The Imitation of Christ. It's made of short chapters, sometimes just a few lines each, the kind you can read in a minute and think about all day. It tells the reader to love being unknown, and to care more about living well than about knowing a lot. It says, in effect, that a humble farmer who serves God is better off than a proud scholar who studies the stars and neglects himself. Its whole aim is in the title: to follow Christ closely, in the heart. The book went out without much fanfare, and in time it found readers far beyond his house, Catholic and Protestant both. There's a saying handed down under Thomas's name, usually given in Latin as in angello cum libello: in a little nook with a little book. He looked for rest everywhere, it says, and found it only there. That's a copyist's line. The Bible has an older one. In Deuteronomy, a king is told that when he takes the throne, in the King James Bible, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book". Not only hear it. Write it, by his own hand.

Here's the practice: copy out one line by hand. Find a pen and a scrap of paper, or the back of an envelope. Pick one line that matters to you: a verse, a line from a prayer you already know, or one from a book that has stayed with you. Write it out slowly, letter by letter, the way Thomas did. Don't hurry. Let your hand go at the speed of attention. When it's finished, read it once in silence. If you pray, you can let it become your prayer for the rest of the sit. If you don't, just stay with the words on the page. The bell holds the time.
Kempis. The quiet copyist and canon of the Modern Devotion, Thomas à Kempis, to whom tradition credits The Imitation of Christ.
Your line: in a nook with a book. Today, find one small corner, a chair, a step, a bench, and spend five quiet minutes there with the line you copied. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: Joan's trial
836.hook: asked if she was in God's grace: if I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may he keep me
836.howItsDone: Catholics honor Joan of Arc as a saint, and her answer about grace is quoted by Christians of different churches as a picture of humble trust before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas à Kempis, copying by hand in his quiet house. Your line was in a nook with a book. Did you find your corner, and your line? Day eight hundred thirty-six.

Do you know if you are in the grace of God? The question comes from across a crowded room in Rouen. Learned men in robes sit in rows: churchmen, doctors of theology, lawyers. In front of them stands a young woman from a farming village, in chains between sessions, who cannot read. She has led soldiers in war, she says, because voices from God told her to. Now she's on trial for her life. And the question is a trap. If she says yes, she sounds proud, as if she could be sure of God's verdict. If she says no, she admits she's not in God's favor, and condemns herself. The room waits. Today: Joan's trial.
screen: `ARE YOU IN THE GRACE OF GOD?`

segments.voice: Joan of Arc grew up in a village in France during a long war with England. She said that saints' voices came to her and told her to help the French king. Somehow she got an audience with him, and then an army, and she rode with it in armor. Later she was captured and handed over to a church court that sided with her enemies. The trial record survives, and her answers in it are startling. Take the moment over grace. As the record gives it, paraphrased: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me there. And she added that she'd be the saddest person in the world if she knew she were not in God's grace. The answer holds, but not by being clever. It doesn't claim to know what only God knows. It doesn't confess what isn't true. It turns the trap into a prayer. In the New Testament, grace is a gift, something nobody earns. The letter to the Ephesians puts it this way in the King James Bible: "For by grace are ye saved through faith". Her answer leaves grace where that verse puts it: in God's hands. Jesus had told his followers what to do when they were brought before councils. In the King James Bible: "take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour". The court condemned her, and she was burned. Years later, a new church inquiry overturned the verdict, and in time the Catholic Church named her a saint.
screen: `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.`
`IT SHALL BE GIVEN YOU IN THAT HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer a trap humbly. Think of a question that's been put to you as a trap. At work. At a family dinner. Online. A question where yes and no both lose. Remember how it went, and what you said. Now, in your mind, try Joan's way. Not proving them wrong. Not giving in. Find an answer that's honest about what you don't know, and humble about what you do. Let it be short. If you pray, you can ask for the right words when the moment comes. If you don't, just rest in the not-knowing for a while. The bell holds the time.
Joan's trial. The church court in Rouen where a young woman from a farming village answered a trap about God's grace with a humble prayer.
Your line: if I am, keep me. Today, when someone asks you a question built to catch you, slow down, and answer the way Joan did: honest, short and humble. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

837.title: Constantinople falls (1453)
837.hook: the last liturgy in Hagia Sophia; the Orthodox world's center shifts north
837.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians remember the fall of Constantinople with sorrow, and the Ecumenical Patriarch, honored by Orthodox Christians as first among their patriarchs, still has his seat in the city, now Istanbul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan's trial, and her careful answer to a trap. Your line was if I am, keep me. Where did a humble answer get you out of a corner? Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Candles, and a great dome overhead, and a crowd that has every reason to be afraid. The walls of the city are under siege. Outside, an army has been pounding them with cannon, day after day. And on the last evening, the old accounts say, the people of Constantinople crowd into their great church for one more service. Greek Christians and Latin Christians, who had quarreled bitterly, stand under the same dome and pray together. Some confess their sins. Some ask forgiveness of the person next to them. Then the soldiers go back to the walls. Today: Constantinople falls.

The church was Hagia Sophia, the name means Holy Wisdom, and for a long time it had been the heart of Eastern Christianity, the seat of the patriarch, the place where emperors were crowned. The army outside belonged to the Ottoman sultan, Mehmed. When the walls broke, the emperor, Constantine, died, the accounts say, fighting at them, and the city that had called itself the new Rome passed into Ottoman hands. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, and before long it was a mosque, with Muslim prayer under the same dome. People still tell a story about that last liturgy. As soldiers burst in, the story goes, a priest at the altar picked up the holy gifts and walked into the wall, and the wall closed behind him. One day, the story says, he will walk out and finish the service. It's told as legend, not as history. It's the kind of story people tell when something unfinished hurts. A Psalm knows that hurt. In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." So what happened to the Orthodox world? It didn't end. It moved its center of gravity. In the north, in Moscow, Russian Christians began to see themselves as carriers of what Constantinople had held. Some there spoke of Moscow as a third Rome. And in the old city itself, Christians stayed. The patriarchate went on, with a new patriarch installed under the new rulers. Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox lived as a minority, with their own churches, keeping their liturgy, generation after generation. The last liturgy in Hagia Sophia was not the last liturgy.
screen: `THE PRIEST WHO WALKED INTO THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold in mind Christians who live as a small community, where their neighbors mostly follow another faith or none. Picture a small church on an ordinary street, a few families coming in for a service, keeping it going year after year. If you know one by name, or someone who belongs to one, bring them to mind. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply wish them well, and wish their neighbors well too. The bell holds the time.
Constantinople falls. The great Christian city of the East passes to the Ottomans, Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque, and Orthodox Christians carry on, in the old city and in the north.
Your line: the last liturgy. Today, when something ends that you loved, notice what keeps going anyway, and give it a little of your attention. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

838.title: Gutenberg's Bible
838.hook: a goldsmith's press in Mainz prints the Bible, and books start to get cheap
838.howItsDone: Christians often give Bibles as gifts at baptisms, confirmations, weddings and graduations, and Bible societies print and give away Bibles in many languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople falls, and the last liturgy under the great dome. Your line was the last liturgy. When something ended, what kept going anyway? Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

A tiny metal letter, the size of a fingernail, standing on its end. A capital I. Next to it, an n. Then another letter, and another, until a whole line of them sits in a wooden frame, backward, like a word seen in a mirror. Ink goes over the line. Paper comes down. A screw turns, the press squeezes, and the page comes up with the words the right way round. Then the letters are taken apart and set again for the next page. In a workshop in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg is doing this with the whole Bible. Today: Gutenberg's Bible.

Before the press, every Bible in Europe was copied by hand, the way we watched Thomas à Kempis do it at his desk. Every copy was its own work, and every copy was precious. Gutenberg's idea was to make the letters movable. Cast them in metal, line them up, print a page, then break them apart and use them again. His Bible was in Latin, the Bible the Western church read in worship, and its Genesis begins with the words the King James Bible gives as: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The printed pages were made to look like the best handwritten books. Two columns, dark, even letters. Copies were often finished by hand, with red headings and painted capitals added after printing, so no two look quite the same. Here's what came next. Once one press worked, others followed, in other cities. Books got cheaper. More people could own one. Later, reformers would print the Bible in German, in English, in the languages people spoke at home, and tracts and sermons would travel fast. Christians argued, sometimes fiercely, over what all those readers should do with what they read. But the change underneath was simple. A Psalm says, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." For a long time, that lamp sat in a church or a library. The press began to put it on kitchen tables.
screen: `COPIED BY HAND, ONE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone a book. Think about the books that changed something for you. Maybe a Bible, maybe a novel, maybe a book of poems someone handed you at the right time. Now think of one person who might need a book right now. A friend, a child, a coworker, someone at your church or on your street. Choose the book, and choose the person. If you pray, you can pray for them as you choose. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Gutenberg's Bible. The Latin Bible printed with movable metal type in Mainz, part of a change that made books, and Bibles, cheaper to own.
Your line: words for everyone. Today, give the book you chose, or lend one off your own shelf, with a short note inside saying why. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

839.title: Lalibela
839.hook: in Ethiopia, churches carved downward out of solid rock
839.howItsDone: Ethiopian Orthodox Christians make pilgrimage to Lalibela, especially at Genna, their Christmas, and at Timkat, the feast of Jesus's baptism, gathering in white shawls in the rock-cut churches to pray and sing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gutenberg's Bible, and metal letters that made books cheap. Your line was words for everyone. Did a book change hands? Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

On a plain of reddish stone in the Ethiopian highlands, at first there seems to be nothing to see. Then the ground opens. At the edge of a deep trench, down at the bottom, its roof level with the plain, stands a church. A whole church, with doors and windows and a cross on top, all one piece with the rock around it. Nobody built it up. Somebody dug it down. Pilgrims in white shawls climb down stone steps into the trenches to pray. Today: Lalibela.

Lalibela is a town in northern Ethiopia, named for a king the Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors as a saint. Tradition says King Lalibela wanted a holy city in his own land, a new Jerusalem, for Christians who could not make the long journey to the old one. And so, the tradition goes, churches were cut out of the living rock. Here's how it worked. The carvers started from the top. They cut a trench around a huge block of stone, leaving it standing free. Then they hollowed the block from the inside: rooms, pillars, arches, windows, all carved out, nothing added. If you cut away too much, there was no putting it back. One church is shaped like a cross when seen from above, its roof flat with the ground. The place carries names from the Holy Land. A stream there is called the Jordan. Ethiopian Christianity has its own way. Its church belongs to the family of Oriental Orthodox churches, with its own language of worship, Ge'ez, its own calendar and its own feasts. At Lalibela, crowds of pilgrims gather at Christmas, which Ethiopian Christians call Genna, filling the trenches and the rock-cut courtyards. Isaiah has a line that fits a church dug into stone. In the King James Bible: "look unto the rock whence ye are hewn." And Jesus, in Matthew, says, "upon this rock I will build my church." At Lalibela, that image becomes stone you can touch. The church isn't set on the rock. It is the rock.
screen: `CUT FROM THE TOP, HOLLOWED FROM INSIDE.`
`NOT ON THE ROCK. IT IS THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carve out one hour. The carvers at Lalibela made room by taking away. Look at the week ahead, in your head or on your phone. Find one hour you could cut free, the way they cut a trench around a block of stone. Early in the morning, a lunch break, an evening without a screen. Choose it. Mark it. If you pray, that hour can be for prayer. If you don't, let it be for quiet, a walk, or a long look at something beautiful. The bell holds the time.
Lalibela. A town in Ethiopia, named for a saint-king, where churches were carved down into solid rock as a new Jerusalem.
Your line: churches in the rock. Today, protect the hour you carved out. When something tries to fill it, say no, once, kindly. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: Nubia's churches
840.hook: Christian kingdoms once flourished on the Nile in what is now Sudan, and their churches were almost forgotten
840.howItsDone: The Nubian churches no longer hold services, but paintings from the cathedral at Faras are kept in museums, and Christians in Sudan and elsewhere sometimes remember the Nubian kingdoms as part of their own story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalibela, where churches were carved down into the rock. Your line was churches in the rock. Did you keep your carved-out hour safe? Day eight hundred forty.

Sand, blown over the ruins of a town by the Nile. Archaeologists dig, and under the sand they find walls, and on the walls, faces. Saints with large dark eyes. Angels. Mary holding her child. A bishop, painted in his robes, looking straight out at them as if he'd been waiting. These are the walls of a cathedral, in a place called Faras, in old Nubia, the land along the Nile south of Egypt. Whole Christian kingdoms once lived here. Their names had mostly faded from memory. Today: Nubia's churches.

The Bible already knows this land, though it calls it Ethiopia, its word for the country south of Egypt. A Psalm says, in the King James Bible, "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." And in Acts, Philip meets on the road "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians." He's reading Isaiah, he asks to be baptized, and he goes on his way rejoicing. Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia. Later, kings along the Nile became Christian, and their kingdoms, Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, built churches and cathedrals, with bishops and monasteries, and walls covered in paintings. They worshiped in Greek and Coptic, and wrote in their own Nubian language too. For a long time they flourished. Then, slowly, the kingdoms weakened, and the churches emptied. There was no single dramatic fall, the way there was at Constantinople. The faith faded out of the valley, and sand covered the walls. And that's why this day matters. Christian history isn't only Rome, Constantinople and the cathedrals of Europe. It reached Africa early, riding home with that traveler from Philip's road, and it grew along the Nile. This week ran from Jan Hus seeking the truth, Thomas à Kempis in his nook, Joan's humble answer, the last liturgy in Hagia Sophia, Gutenberg's letters, churches in the rock at Lalibela, and now faces under the sand. To remember a church is to say: these people were here, and they prayed.

Here's the practice: learn one lost church's name. Say the kingdoms' names slowly, once each: Nobadia. Makuria. Alodia. Then the town: Faras. Picture the painted bishop on the wall, the saints with their wide eyes, the people who once stood in front of them on an ordinary morning. You don't know their names. You can hold them for a minute anyway. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, let the names be enough. The bell holds the time.
